plain_text: IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF THE STATE OF IDAHO                                         Docket No. 52189   RE/MAX PRESTIGE, a real estate                 )  brokerage, and its broker, DAREN               ) Filed: March 6, 2026  LONG,                                          )                                                 ) Melanie Gagnepain, Clerk         Plaintiffs-Respondents,                 )                                                 )  v.                                             )                                                 )  SUSAN L. MATTSON,                              )                                                 )         Defendant-Appellant.                    )                                                 )         Appeal from the District Court of the Seventh Judicial District, State of Idaho,        Bingham County. Hon. Darren B. Simpson, District Judge.         Judgment awarding damages, interest, costs, and attorney fees for breach of        contract, affirmed.         Blaser Oleson & Lloyd, Chtd.; Jeromy W. Pharis, Blackfoot, for appellant.         Carey Law, PLLC; Donald F. Carey, Idaho Falls, for respondents.                 ________________________________________________ LORELLO, Judge        Susan L. Mattson appeals from the district courtâs judgment awarding damages, interest, costs, and attorney fees for breach of contract. We affirm.                                                 I.                      FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND        Mattson owns a parcel of real property in Bingham County, which she wished to sell to a buyer intending to keep the property as farmland. On September 15, 2022, Mattson entered into a seller-representation agreement (the contract) for a term of six months with Connie Clawson, acting as the agent for the broker, and Daren Long, acting as the broker of Re/Max Prestige. The contract stated, âSELLER, Susan L. Mattson retains Daren Long, Broker of RE/Max Prestige as                                                     1 SELLERâS exclusive Broker to sell.â The contract further provided that Mattson agreed to sell the property for $360,000, and stated:                 [6] (A) If Broker or any person, including SELLER, procures a purchaser        ready, willing and able to purchase, transfer or exchange the Property on the terms        stated herein, or on any other price and terms agreed to in writing, the SELLER        agrees to pay a total brokerage fee of 6% of the contract or purchase price . . . Of        this total brokerage fee, 3% of the contract price will be shared with the cooperating        brokerage unless otherwise agreed to in writing.        On September 19, Mattson informed Clawson that Justin Oleson wanted to purchase the property. Clawson spoke with Oleson on the phone that day and he expressed a belief that the property was only worth $200,000. Oleson accused Clawson of listing the property for $360,000 because she intended to sell the property to be developed, rather than seeking a buyer intending to use the property to farm as Mattson desired. Clawson responded that was not the case and that she would inform Mattson that Oleson was not interested in purchasing the property. Shortly after this phone call, Oleson went to Mattsonâs house, after which they executed a handwritten agreement signed by Mattson, Oleson, and Mattsonâs brother, agreeing that Mattson would sell Oleson the property for $200,000. Communications subsequently broke down between Clawson and Oleson, at which time Clawson directed Oleson to direct any future communications regarding the property to Long.        On September 21, Clawson presented Mattson with an offer from another buyer to purchase the property for the full listing price of $360,000. This buyer was utilizing a loan program that required the property to be used as farmland to satisfy Mattsonâs wishes. However, Mattson never accepted the offer or inquired about the buyerâs intended use of the property and, instead, expressed her intent to ask Oleson to increase his offer price.        Over a series of emails exchanged between September 21 and September 26, Long inquired as to whether Oleson intended to âprepare a more formal and legible purchase agreementâ as he was, at the time, a licensed attorney.1 Oleson did not respond to this inquiry. On March 16, 2023, Re/Max Prestige and Long filed a complaint against Mattson for breach of contract, seeking to recover the 6 percent commission based on the $360,000 offer, which amount totaled $21,600. A bench trial was subsequently held. At the conclusion of evidence, Mattson moved to dismiss the   1        Oleson was disbarred from the Idaho State Bar on April 4, 2025.                                                   2 action arguing Re/Max Prestige and Long did not have standing. The district court ordered the parties to submit supplemental briefing on this issue.        Re/Max Prestige and Long filed motions to substitute or amend the complaint to include All-Around Realty, LLC, as a real party in interest. Mattson opposed these motions. The district court subsequently held a hearing and issued findings of fact and conclusions of law. The district court found Mattson breached the contract and Long was entitled to recover $21,600 in commission fees from Mattson. Mattson filed a motion to reconsider, which the district court denied. The district court then entered the judgment, which included an award of costs and attorney fees to Re/Max Prestige and Long, as well as pre- and post-judgment interest on the damages previously awarded. Mattson appeals.                                                   II.                                     STANDARD OF REVIEW        Where a trial court sits as a finder of fact without a jury the court is required to enter findings of fact and conclusions of law. I.R.C.P. 52(a); Est. of Hull v. Williams, 126 Idaho 437, 440, 885 P.2d 1153, 1156 (Ct. App. 1994). Our review of the trial courtâs decision is limited to ascertaining whether substantial, competent evidence supports the findings of fact, and whether the trial court correctly applied the law to the facts as found. Borah v. McCandless, 147 Idaho 73, 77, 205 P.3d 1209, 1213 (2009); Cummings v. Cummings, 115 Idaho 186, 188, 765 P.2d 697, 699 (Ct. App. 1988). Thus, we defer to findings of fact that are not clearly erroneous, but we freely review the trial courtâs conclusions of law reached by applying the facts found to the applicable law. Staggie v. Idaho Falls Consol. Hosps., 110 Idaho 349, 351, 715 P.2d 1019, 1021 (Ct. App. 1986). Where there is conflicting evidence, it is the trial courtâs task to evaluate the credibility of witnesses and to weigh the evidence presented. Desfosses v. Desfosses, 120 Idaho 354, 357, 815 P.2d 1094, 1097 (Ct. App. 1991). We will not set aside the trial courtâs factual findings as clearly erroneous if they are supported by substantial and competent, even if conflicting, evidence. Kennedy v. Schneider, 151 Idaho 440, 442, 259 P.3d 586, 588 (2011). Evidence is substantial and competent if a reasonable trier of fact would accept that evidence and rely on it to determine whether a disputed point of fact was proven. Hull v. Giesler, 156 Idaho 765, 772, 331 P.3d 507, 514 (2014); Hutchison v. Anderson, 130 Idaho 936, 940, 950 P.2d 1275, 1279 (Ct. App. 1997).                                                       3                                                  III.                                             ANALYSIS          Mattson argues that Re/Max Prestige lacked standing to file the underlying lawsuit because Re/Max Prestige is an assumed business name for All-Around Realty that is not properly registered with the Idaho Secretary of State and thus not a separate legal entity with standing to sue. While the district court took judicial notice of the legal relationship between Re/Max Prestige, Long and All-Around Realty, Mattson asserts this was error. Mattson further contends that Long did not have standing because he is not listed as a designated broker of Re/Max Prestige. Mattson argues the district court erred in concluding that Re/Max Prestige and Long did not breach their statutory duties owed to Mattson regarding the formation of a contract with Oleson. Finally, Mattson argues that, in the event this Court holds that the district court correctly denied her motion to dismiss, the district court erred in calculating damages awarded to Re/Max Prestige and Long. In response, Re/Max Prestige and Long assert the record reflects that: the district court did not err in denying Mattsonâs motion to dismiss for lack of standing; the district court did not err in concluding that Re/Max Prestige and Long did not breach any statutory duties; the district court correctly calculated damages; this appeal is frivolous; and Re/Max Prestige and Long are entitled to costs and attorney fees on appeal. We hold that Mattson has failed to show any error by the district court. A.       Judicial Notice          A trial courtâs decision to take judicial notice under I.R.E. 201 is an evidentiary ruling, which we review for an abuse of discretion. Chaput v. State, 168 Idaho 774, 777, 487 P.3d 366, 369 (2021); Rome v. State, 164 Idaho 407, 413, 431 P.3d 242, 248 (2018). When a trial courtâs discretionary decision is reviewed on appeal, the appellate court conducts a multi-tiered inquiry to determine whether the trial court: (1) correctly perceived the issue as one of discretion; (2) acted within the boundaries of such discretion; (3) acted consistently with any legal standards applicable to the specific choices before it; and (4) reached its decision by an exercise of reason. Lunneborg v. My Fun Life, 163 Idaho 856, 863, 421 P.3d 187, 194 (2018).          Idaho Rule of Evidence 201 allows a court to judicially notice a fact that is not subject to reasonable dispute because it âcan be accurately and readily determined from sources whose                                                       4 accuracy cannot reasonably be questioned.â I.R.E. 201(b)(2). A party is âentitled to be heard on the propriety of taking judicial notice and the nature of the fact to be noticed.â I.R.E. 201(e).         On appeal, Mattson contends the district court abused its discretion by misstating the legal relationship between Re/Max Prestige, Long, and All-Around Realty. At the conclusion of the trial, the district court stated:                  This Court takes judicial notice of the fact that in the records of Idahoâs         Secretary of State, Long is the designated broker for All-Around Realty, L.L.C.,         doing business as Re/Max Prestige. Within the same record, [Clawson] and Long         are listed as the managers of All-Around Realty, L.L.C. [Clawsonâs husband] is         listed as a member of All-Around Realty, L.L.C. [Clawson and her husband] do         business under the assumed name Re/Max Prestige. (footnotes omitted). In addition, the district court took judicial notice that âLongâs license with the Idaho Real Estate Commission lists him as the designated broker for All-Around Realty, L.L.C., which does business as Re/Max Prestige.â The language of I.R.E. 201(e) provides that a party making a timely request âis entitled to be heard on the propriety of taking judicial notice and the nature of the fact to be noticed.â Additionally, if the trial court âtakes judicial notice before notifying a party, the party on request is still entitled to be heard.â I.R.E. 201(e). Trial courts should construe the rules so as to âadminister every proceeding fairly, eliminate unjustifiable expense and delay, and promote the development of evidence law, to the end of ascertaining the truth and securing a just determination.â I.R.E. 102.         Under the plain language of I.R.E. 201(e), a party challenging the propriety of a trial courtâs judicial notice and the nature of the facts the trial court noticed is required to request a hearing on the matter. Such a request gives the trial court the opportunity to rule on the partyâs challenge. This decision in turn forms the basis for appellate review. Absent a request to be heard on a challenge, the party fails to preserve the issue for appeal. Chaput, 168 Idaho at 778, 487 P.3d at 370.         Mattson did not challenge the district courtâs judicial notice and thus failed to preserve the issue for appeal. Mattson had the opportunity to challenge the district courtâs judicial notice during the hearing on the motion for reconsideration. Regardless, any possible error was inconsequential. Idaho Rule of Civil Procedure 61 provides that, unless justice otherwise requires, no error in admitting evidence is grounds for vacating, modifying, or otherwise disturbing a judgment or order. âAt every stage of the proceeding, the court must disregard all errors and defects that do                                                     5 not affect any partyâs substantial rights.â Id. In this case, the district courtâs possible error in interpreting the legal relationship between Re/Max Prestige, Long, and All-Around Realty was inconsequential because, as explained below, Long had standing to bring this suit, both as a real party in interest and as a representative of Re/Max Prestige. B.       Standing          To satisfy the requirement of standing, a litigant must allege an injury in fact, a fairly traceable causal connection between the claimed injury and the challenged conduct, and a substantial likelihood that the judicial relief requested will prevent or redress the claimed injury. Sec. Fin. Fund, LLC v. Thomason, 153 Idaho 343, 347, 282 P.3d 604, 608 (2012). An action must be brought in the name of the real party in interest. Id. Idaho Rule of Civil Procedure 17(a)(1)(G) allows a party âwith whom or in whose name a contract has been made for anotherâs benefitâ to prosecute an action in âtheir own name without joining the person for whose benefit the action is brought.â Whether a party has standing as the real party in interest is an issue that may be raised at any time. Med. Recovery Servs., LLC v. Eddins, 169 Idaho 236, 242, 494 P.3d 784, 790 (2021). Idaho Rule of Civil Procedure 17(a)(3) provides that a trial court âmay not dismiss an action for failure to prosecute in the name of the real party in interest until, after an objection, a reasonable time has been allowed for the real party in interest to ratify, join, or be substituted into the action.â Once ratification, joinder, or substitution occurs, âthe action proceeds as if it had been originally commenced by the real party in interest.â I.R.C.P. 17(a)(3). Jurisdictional issues, like standing, are questions of law. Med. Recovery Servs. LLC, 169 Idaho at 242, 494 P.3d at 790. Over questions of law, we exercise free review. Kawai Farms, Inc. v. Longstreet, 121 Idaho 610, 613, 826 P.2d 1322, 1325 (1992); Cole v. Kunzler, 115 Idaho 552, 555, 768 P.2d 815, 818 (Ct. App. 1989).          Mattson contends that Long lacks standing because he was not correctly listed as a broker for Re/Max Prestige on the filings with the Idaho Secretary of State. However, Long is a party to the contract at issue, as it states âSELLER, [Mattson] retains [Long], Broker of Re/Max Prestige as SELLERâS exclusive Broker to sell.â Pursuant to I.C. Â§ 54-2083(4), a âbrokerageâ is defined as a âlicensed designated broker, the licensed real estate business represented by that broker and its associated licensees.â A âdesignated brokerâ is defined as âan individual who is licensed as a real estate broker in Idaho and who is designated by the brokerage company to be responsible for                                                      6 the supervision of the brokerage company and the activities of any associated licensees in accordance with this chapter.â I.C. Â§ 54-2083(9). The broker is responsible for executing a brokerage representation agreement that meets the minimum qualifications set forth in I.C. Â§ 54- 2050.         In this case, the contract was a brokerage representation agreement as described in I.C. Â§ 54-2050. Mattson violated the contract when she agreed to sell the property to Oleson during the contract period with Long. According to the contract, Long was entitled to a commission for the sale of the property and, as such, suffered an injury in fact when Mattson breached the contract.         Mattson also asserts that Re/Max Prestige does not have standing because it is not a separate legal entity. Clawson is listed with the Idaho Secretary of State as doing business as Re/Max Prestige. However, as Clawson is a party to the contract, and is listed as doing business as Re/Max Prestige, she also had standing to sue for violation of the contract. Furthermore, Long had standing to bring a suit on behalf of Re/Max Prestige under I.R.C.P. 17 as the representative of a party for whom the contract was made to benefit. Even if the district court erred in its description of the legal relationship between the involved entities, both Long and Re/Max Prestige are appropriate plaintiffs with standing to sue on the breach of contract claim against Mattson. C.      Breach of Statutory Duties         Mattson claims the district court failed to recognize that Re/Max Prestige and Long breached duties owed to Mattson as set forth in I.C. Â§Â§ 54-2083, 54-2086, and 54-2087. Mattson contends that, pursuant to I.C. Â§ 54-2083(7), Oleson was a customer, which is defined in the statute as âa buyer or seller, or prospective buyer or seller, who is not represented in an agency relationship in a regulated real estate transaction.â Mattson relies on I.C. Â§ 54-2086(1)(a), which states that a brokerage and its licensees owe a duty to âperform ministerial acts to assist the buyer or seller in the sale or purchase of real estate.â Ministerial acts refer to âreasonably necessary and customary acts typically performed by real estate licensees in assisting a transaction to its closing or conclusion.â I.C. Â§ 54-2083(12). These duties owed to a customer âare mandatory and may not be waived or abrogated, either unilaterally or by agreement.â I.C. Â§ 54-2086(3),         The district court correctly concluded that this argument is meritless because Long communicated over email with Oleson and attempted to ascertain who would draft the contract. Long, as the broker, asked Oleson if, as an attorney, he planned to draft a formal contract for the                                                     7 property sale. In the alternative, Long offered to have someone from the Re/Max Prestige office draft the contract. Mattson argues that, regardless of Olesonâs failure to respond, Long still breached a duty by failing to take affirmative action and draft a contract for the sale of the property. On appeal, Oleson and Mattson appear to have presented an expectation that Long would use the partially illegible napkin agreement, written by Oleson at Mattsonâs home without Long present, to draft a final contract for the sale of the property. Mattson contends that, because of this failure, Long is no longer entitled to the commission for the sale. This is an inaccurate representation of the events that took place. Long attempted to communicate with Oleson and offered to draft the property sale contract. Oleson did not respond to these requests.2 Long was not present at the meeting between Oleson and Mattson and thus could not accurately depict their desired terms without further communication from both of them. Oleson initially reached out to Clawson and Long to purchase the property and only pursued Mattson privately after he expressed dissatisfaction with the asking price. Long and Re/Max Prestige procured a buyer for Mattsonâs property who was willing to pay the asking price of $360,000 and to maintain the property as farmland.3 Mattsonâs failure to comply with the contract does not excuse her from paying the commission to Long and Re/Max Prestige as required by the contract.    2          Idaho Rule of Professional Conduct 5.7 states that a lawyer shall be subject to the Rules of Professional Conduct with respect to the provision of law-related services if the law-related services are provided: (1) by the lawyer in circumstances that are not distinct from the lawyerâs provision of legal services to clients; or (2) by a separate entity controlled by the lawyer individually or with others if the lawyer fails to take reasonable measures to assure that a person obtaining the law-related services knows that the services of the separate entity are not legal services and that the protections of the client-lawyer relationship do not exist. Comment 9 to this rule lists such law-related services which includes real estate counseling. Mattson argues that a duty was breached by Long. However, it remains unclear based on the emails from Oleson conveying Mattsonâs desires to Long and Re/Max Prestige if Oleson was also attempting to represent Mattson as an attorney in her communications with the brokerage. Oleson was using his firm email address and representing Mattsonâs wishes to Long and Re/Max Prestige in an ambiguous fashion. 3        It is worth noting that, regardless of the potential to legally enforce any such provision, there was nothing legible in the agreement between Mattson and Oleson that stipulated the property would remain undeveloped, in spite of the transferable division rights attached to the property. Olesonâs oral promise to Mattson that the property would remain undeveloped would                                                     8 D.     Calculation of Damages        In an action for breach of contract, only such damages will be allowed as fairly compensate the injured party for his loss. Gilbert v. City of Caldwell, 112 Idaho 386, 395, 732 P.2d 355, 364 (Ct. App. 1987). The law of damages in breach of contract claims seeks to place the aggrieved party in the same economic position the party would have had if the contract had been performed. Id. The determination of the correct measure of damages is a question of law this Court reviews de novo. Gen. Auto Parts Co., Inc. v. Genuine Parts Co., 132 Idaho 849, 854, 979 P.2d 1207, 1212 (1999); see Basic Am., Inc. v. Shatila, 133 Idaho 726, 745, 992 P.2d 175, 194 (1999).        Mattson argues that the damages calculated by the district court were inaccurate. Mattson contends that Long and Re/Max Prestige were only entitled to 3 percent of the $360,000, rather than the 6 percent awarded by the district court. A broker earns a commission when he or she procures a buyer who is ready, willing, and able to purchase on terms acceptable to the seller. Strout Realty, Inc. v. Milhous, 107 Idaho 330, 332, 689 P.2d 222, 224 (Ct. App. 1984). Whether a ready, willing, and able buyer has been produced is a question of fact on which the broker bears the burden of proof. Id. If the failure of completion of the contract results from a wrongful act or interference of the seller, the brokerâs claim is valid and must be paid. Margaret H. Wayne Tr. v. Lipsky, 123 Idaho 253, 260, 846 P.2d 904, 906 (1993).        The district court awarded 6 percent of $360,000, which was the bargained-for commission Mattson agreed to in the contract. The district court concluded that Long was entitled to receive the commission percentage based on the listing price, which had been offered by the prospective buyer procured by Re/Max Prestige and Long. The offer for $360,000 served as proof that Oleson was mistaken in his representation of the value of the property. Mattson argues that, because the prospective buyers were represented by another brokerage, Re/Max Prestige and Long would have only received 3 percent under the contract, with the other 3 percent commission awarded to the participating brokerage representing the buyer.        As the district court correctly concluded, Long was owed 6 percent commission for successfully procuring a desirable buyer for Mattson. The commission became due when Mattson    be unenforceable because it was not included in their handwritten agreement. See I.C. Â§ 9-503 to I.C. Â§ 9-505.                                                    9 breached the contract. Whether Re/Max Prestige and Long kept all 6 percent or owed 3 percent to a cooperating brokerage is a question that arose after Mattson breached by contracting with Oleson to sell the property without Long. To put Re/Max Prestige and Long in the same economic position they would have been in had the contract been performed requires awarding the 6 percent commission rate agreed to in the contract. The district court did not err in calculating the award of damages. E.      Costs and Attorney Fees on Appeal         Mattson argues that she is entitled to costs and attorney fees on appeal. Because Mattson is not the prevailing party on appeal, she is not entitled to an award of costs or attorney fees.         Re/Max Prestige and Long also request attorney fees on appeal, arguing that Mattsonâs appeal is frivolous. Pursuant to I.C. Â§ 12-121 and I.A.R. 41, an award of attorney fees may be granted to the prevailing party and such an award is appropriate when the court finds that the appeal has been brought or defended frivolously, unreasonably, or without foundation. An award of attorney fees is appropriate if the appellant only invites this Court to second-guess the trial court on conflicting evidence, or if the law is well settled and the appellant has made no substantial showing that the lower court misapplied the law, or no cogent challenge is presented with regard to the trial courtâs exercise of discretion. Pass v. Kenny, 118 Idaho 445, 449-50, 797 P.2d 153, 157-58 (Ct. App. 1990). This standard is satisfied in this case. Accordingly, Re/Max Prestige and Long are entitled to costs and attorney fees on appeal.                                                   IV.                                           CONCLUSION         Mattson has failed to show that Re/Max Prestige and Long lacked standing, that they breached a statutory duty, or that the district court erred in calculating damages. Accordingly, the district courtâs judgment awarding damages, interest, costs, and attorney fees for breach of contract is affirmed. Costs and attorney fees are awarded to Re/Max Prestige and Long on appeal.         Judge HUSKEY and Judge Pro Tem MELANSON, CONCUR.                                                       10

court: Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
plain_text: USCA11 Case: 23-10123     Document: 44-1       Date Filed: 10/03/2025      Page: 1 of 18                                     FOR PUBLICATION                                        In the                  United States Court of Appeals                           For the Eleventh Circuit                             ____________________                                     No. 23-10123                             ____________________          CATRELL IVORY,                                                            Petitioner-Appellant,         versus          UNITED STATES OF AMERICA,                                                           Respondent-Appellee.                             ____________________                      Appeal from the United States District Court                           for the Middle District of Florida                       D.C. Docket No. 6:21-cv-01138-PGB-LHP                             ____________________          Before JILL PRYOR, GRANT, and MARCUS, Circuit Judges.         GRANT, Circuit Judge:                Catrell Ivory and two accomplices spent the summer of 2017         robbing Walmart stores at gunpoint. All told, the crew made out USCA11 Case: 23-10123      Document: 44-1      Date Filed: 10/03/2025     Page: 2 of 18             2                      Opinion of the Court                 23-10123          with about $100,000. Nothing good lasts forever, though, and po-         lice eventually arrested everyone involved. Despite a mountain of         evidence against him, Ivory maintained his innocence, declined         multiple plea oï¬ers, and opted for trial. That decision aged poorly:         a jury convicted him of ï¬ve robbery and gun charges, and a judge         sentenced him to 319 monthsâ imprisonment.                 Ivory ï¬rst appealed his convictions in 2019, and we aï¬rmed         them in a single paragraph because there were âno arguable issues         of merit.â Even so, he now seeks to vacate his convictions on the         ground that he received ineï¬ective assistance of counsel at trial. He         begins with an about-face regarding his innocence. Ivory now ad-         mits that he did, in fact, participate in some of the robberies, and         he faults his attorney for encouraging him to reject the govern-         mentâs plea oï¬ers. On top of that, he says that his attorneyâs per-         formance was separately defective because she failed to call his         cousinâone of his fellow robbersâas a witness to testify on his         behalf.                  We are unpersuaded. While we make no excuses for the         poor performance of Ivoryâs counsel, none of her errors prejudiced         Ivory. And because we cannot say that there is a substantial proba-         bility that the result of Ivoryâs trial would have been diï¬erent with-         out his attorneyâs errors, we aï¬rm. USCA11 Case: 23-10123      Document: 44-1     Date Filed: 10/03/2025     Page: 3 of 18             23-10123               Opinion of the Court                        3                                           I.                 This appeal presents a story in three parts: the Walmart rob-         beries, the criminal case, and the follow-on habeas proceedings.         We address each in turn.                                          A.                  In the summer of 2017, Catrell Ivory committed two armed         robberiesâand attempted to commit one moreâat three different         Walmart stores in Florida. Each robbery followed the same         pattern: three masked men clad in black and carrying guns would         storm into an unlucky Walmart sometime around midnight. Once         the robbers entered the store, one of them stood guard near the         entrance while the other two found the store manager and forced         him to âaccess the cash receptacle.â After those two robbers         grabbed the money, they would rejoin the third at the entrance,         and the whole trio would flee in a stolen car. They would then         ditch the vehicle, split the proceeds, and âreturn to their regular         lives.â                The first robbery occurred shortly after midnight on June 2,         2017. Inside the store, Ivory held a gun to a managerâs head while         one of the other robbers pressed his own gun into another         managerâs back. The crew wanted the storeâs moneyâand they         got about $75,000 of it. As the three men left, one of them fired his         gun âin the direction ofâ a random employee. The shot missed,         and the group made its escape in a stolen Ford Edge. USCA11 Case: 23-10123     Document: 44-1     Date Filed: 10/03/2025    Page: 4 of 18             4                     Opinion of the Court                23-10123                  Two months later, the crew struck again. All three robbers         were brandishing guns, and this time they forced shoppers to lie         down on the ground as the robbery unfolded. As for Ivory, his role         was to stand near the entrance and train his gun at the hostages to         keep them still. Though the manager could not access the storeâs         safe, the robbers still made out with about $25,000 after the         manager emptied a âcash recycler machine.â Money in hand, they         fled in another stolen car: this time, a Chevy Malibu.                 Having twice tasted success, the men attempted to rob a         third Walmart eleven days later. The crew was once again masked,         gloved, and armed. When they entered the store, each assailant         forced multiple customers to the ground at gunpoint. But their         heist was unsuccessfulâthe robbers could not find a manager to         open the safe. Empty-handed, they fled in a stolen Honda Civic.                 When police investigated this string of robberies, they         connected the stolen Ford Edge from the first robbery to a man         named Bakari McCant, who is Ivoryâs cousin. Less than a week         after the attempted third robbery, law enforcement arrested         McCant along with two other menâJarvis Wingster and DeAndre         Brewerâas they were casing yet another Walmart. The         government charged McCant with crimes related to the first and         second robberies, and all three men with crimes related to the         attempted fourth. No one faced charges for the third.                 After arresting those three, law enforcement turned its         sights on Ivory, who has his cousin McCant to thank for that. USCA11 Case: 23-10123       Document: 44-1      Date Filed: 10/03/2025      Page: 5 of 18             23-10123                Opinion of the Court                          5          McCantâs first call after his arrest was to his auntâIvoryâs mother.         During the call, McCant said that he needed Ivoryâs mother to âtell         that boy to stay where the fuck he at.â It is undisputed that Ivory         is âthat boy.â Ivoryâs mother obliged and told her son to lie low.                  Wingster, one of the other two arrestees, chose to cooperate         with the government and further implicated Ivory. He told         investigators point-blank that he, McCant, and Ivory robbed the         first two Walmart stores. And even without Wingsterâs confession,         cell-phone location data put Ivory near the Walmarts that were         targeted in the second and third robberies.                Given this evidence, a grand jury indicted Ivory on five         robbery and gun charges.                                            B.                 Ivory hired Nicole Blair Dickerson to represent him at trial.         She has since been disbarred in Florida for general dereliction of         duty. See Formal Complaint for Reciprocal Discipline at 4, Florida         Bar v. Dickerson, No. SC19-616 (Fla. Apr. 16, 2019); Florida Bar v.         Dickerson, No. SC20-1452, 2020 WL 6703176, at *1 (Fla. Nov. 16,         2020).                 Ivoryâs case was set for trial in January 2019. Before trial, the         government offered him two plea deals, but he declined them         both. Ivory later explained that even though he didnât want to put         his family through the stress of a trial, his âmind wouldnât let [him]         admit to something [he] didnât do.â Ivory insisted that he was USCA11 Case: 23-10123       Document: 44-1       Date Filed: 10/03/2025      Page: 6 of 18             6                       Opinion of the Court                   23-10123          completely innocent and that he had an alibi for each of the three         robberies. And he added that Wingster was a âsneaky personâ who         had simply âliedâ when he pointed the finger at Ivory.                  A week before trial, Ivoryâs attorney filed a writ of habeas         corpus ad testificandum to transport McCant from prison in West         Virginia to Florida to testify on Ivoryâs behalf. The court denied         the motion, explaining that Ivoryâs attorney had âunduly delayed         in requesting the writ,â and that the late request provided         âinsufficient timeâ to work out the logistics of transporting McCant         to Florida. Ivoryâs attorney responded by moving to continue the         trial so that McCant could testify, claiming that McCantâs         testimony was âabsolutely necessaryâ to Ivoryâs defense. The         court denied that motion too. It explained that because McCant         still needed to talk to his own attorney about the ramifications of         testifying at Ivoryâs trial, it was unclear whether he would testify at         all. The court also underscored the serious âpotential Fifth         Amendment impediments to Mr. McCant providing testimony.â 1                 The morning of trial, Ivoryâs attorney filed a renewed         motion to continue. Because of the governmentâs delay in         disclosing certain cell-site-data evidence, she said, Ivoryâs rebuttal         expert would be unable to review the evidence in time to testify.         The court denied this motion as well.           1 The district court also chastised Ivoryâs attorney for âdelaying in the         preparation ofâ her case. USCA11 Case: 23-10123      Document: 44-1     Date Filed: 10/03/2025     Page: 7 of 18             23-10123               Opinion of the Court                        7                The trial did not go well for Ivory. Wingster testified that it         was he, McCant, and Ivory who robbed the first Walmart.         Wingster described how he stayed at the front of the store and         made the Walmart employees lie on the ground at gunpoint, while         McCant and Ivory looted the storeâs safe. A few minutes after the         robbery began, he explained, Ivory fled with the money and         McCant ran out behind him while firing his gun into the store.         Wingster also walked the jury through the Walmart security         footage and pointed out which one of the masked men was Ivory.                 He went on to testify that he robbed the second Walmart         with Ivory and McCant too. This time, he âmade sureâ that he was         one of the people physically securing the money because he felt         that he had been shortchanged last time. So Ivory served as the         hostage controller: he was in charge of forcing everyone to lie         down on the ground while the other two collected the cash. After         explaining the role of each participant, Wingster again identified         Ivory on the surveillance footage.                 Also on the stand was an FBI cellular analyst, who testified         that Ivoryâs phone connected to a cell tower near the second         Walmart and explained that his phone pinged from that location         no less than eight times during the robbery. And on the night that         the group attempted the third robbery, the analyst added, Ivoryâs         phone repeatedly connected to a cell tower near the targeted         Walmart. Ivory at first denied that the phone was hisââhell, no,â         he told an FBI agentâbut he admitted at trial that it was one of his         âdrug phones.â USCA11 Case: 23-10123      Document: 44-1      Date Filed: 10/03/2025     Page: 8 of 18             8                      Opinion of the Court                 23-10123                 While the government did not present cell-site evidence         tying Ivory to the first robbery, it had plenty of evidence to prove         the point. On the day before that heist, Wingster called McCant         fifteen times and Ivory six times. And an FBI examiner explained         that this barrage of calls was of a âsignificantly higher volumeâ than         in the months before. Adding to the suspicious nature of the calls,         Wingster tried to place them from an âunknownâ number by         dialing star 67 to conceal his real number.                 In the face of all this evidence, Ivory took the witness stand         and maintained his absolute innocence. Specifically, he claimed         that he could not have possibly committed the robberies because         he had an alibi: he was with his girlfriend during the first robbery         and was selling marijuana during the other two. As for his cell         phoneâthe one that pinged the cell towers near two of the         Walmart locationsâIvory explained that he shared it with McCant         and Wingster. Wingsterâs testimony? Simply âfabricated.â The         jury didnât buy it and found Ivory guilty on all counts.                 Next came sentencing. At his hearing, Ivory stated under         oath that he declined the governmentâs plea offers because his         âmind wouldnât let [him] admit to something [he] didnât do.â He         urged the court to give him âanother chanceââhe again insisted         on his complete innocence, swearing that it âwas not [him] in those         robberiesâ and claiming that Wingster had âliedâ at trial. The court         was unmoved and sentenced him to 319 monthsâ imprisonment. USCA11 Case: 23-10123      Document: 44-1      Date Filed: 10/03/2025     Page: 9 of 18             23-10123               Opinion of the Court                         9                 Ivory appealed the conviction and sentence. But his         appellate counsel moved to withdraw, explaining that there were         no arguable issues for appellate review. See Anders v. California, 386         U.S. 738 (1967). After examining the record, we granted counselâs         motion to withdraw and affirmed.                                           C.                  A little over a year later, Ivory (with the benefit of new         counsel) challenged the lawfulness of his conviction under 28         U.S.C. Â§ 2255. Among other things, he contended that his trial         attorney provided ineffective assistance of counsel. First, he said         that she made misrepresentations that induced him to reject         favorable plea offers from the government. Second, he maintained         that his lawyerâs failure to call McCant as a witness at trial was         deficient performance that prejudiced him. If McCant had testified,         Ivory insisted, then there would have been a reasonable probability         that the jury would have acquitted him on the counts dealing with         the first robbery.                As an exhibit to his motion, Ivory attached a letter from         McCant. In the letter, McCant stated that Ivoryâs attorney never         contacted him about the case. He wrote that he would have         provided the following testimony had he been contacted:             â¢ âCatrell Ivory was not involved in [the first] robbery in              any manner, not in the planning or participation.â USCA11 Case: 23-10123      Document: 44-1      Date Filed: 10/03/2025    Page: 10 of 18             10                     Opinion of the Court                 23-10123               â¢ âI had possession of [Ivoryâs] phone July 30â31st [the                second robbery].â              â¢ âThat phone was passed around to multiple people                including . . . myself, Jarvis Wingster & Catrell Ivory.â              â¢ âBoth jail phone calls to my auntââIvoryâs motherâ                âwere only related to marijuna [sic] and a small amount                of money related to marijuna [sic] sales.â                  The district court rejected Ivoryâs motion without holding         an evidentiary hearing, and it denied him a certiï¬cate of appeala-         bility. Ivory sought to appeal the decision, and this Court agreed         to hear him on two issues. First, whether the district court erred in         denyingâwithout an evidentiary hearingâIvoryâs claim that his         attorney improperly induced him to reject his plea oï¬ers. Second,         whether the district court erred in determiningâagain without an         evidentiary hearingâthat Ivory was not entitled to relief based on         his attorneyâs failure to secure McCant as a witness.                  We answer each question in the negative.                                          II.                 We review a district courtâs decision to deny an evidentiary         hearing for abuse of discretion. Winthrop-Redin v. United States, 767         F.3d 1210, 1215 (11th Cir. 2014). We will reverse only if the district         court applied an âincorrect legal standard,â applied the law in an         âunreasonable or incorrect manner,â followed âimproper         proceduresâ in making its decision, or made factual ï¬ndings that         are âclearly erroneous.â Id. (quotation omitted). USCA11 Case: 23-10123      Document: 44-1       Date Filed: 10/03/2025    Page: 11 of 18             23-10123               Opinion of the Court                         11                                           III.                                            A.                 We begin with Ivoryâs claim that his trial counsel was         ineï¬ective because she âimproperly inducedâ him to reject         favorable plea oï¬ers. Speciï¬cally, Ivory maintains that his Sixth         Amendment right to counsel was violated because his attorney told         him that she had secured two witnesses to testify on his behalf         when, in fact, she had done no such thing. He insists that this         conduct was constitutionally deï¬cient because if his attorney had         not misled him about these witnesses, then he would have pleaded         guilty and received a shorter sentence. The district court rejected         that argument without holding an evidentiary hearing. It was         within its discretion to do so.                  Federal prisoners may challenge the legality of their         convictions and sentences under 28 U.S.C. Â§ 2255, the ânew and         more eï¬cient statutory substitute for habeas corpus.â Nancy J.         King & Joseph L. Hoï¬mann, Habeas for the Twenty-First Century 10         (2011). If there has been a âdenial or infringement of the         constitutional rights of the prisoner,â then we âvacate and set the         judgment aside.â 28 U.S.C. Â§ 2255(b). A prisoner seeking such         relief is entitled to an evidentiary hearing if he âalleges facts that,         if true, would entitle him to relief.â Winthrop-Redin, 767 F.3d at         1216 (quotation omitted); see also 28 U.S.C. Â§ 2255(b). He âneed         only allegeânot proveâreasonably speciï¬c, non-conclusory facts         that, if true, would entitle him to relief.â Winthrop-Redin, 767 F.3d USCA11 Case: 23-10123     Document: 44-1      Date Filed: 10/03/2025     Page: 12 of 18             12                     Opinion of the Court                 23-10123          at 1216 (quotation omitted). But no hearing is required for         allegations that are âpatently frivolous, based upon unsupported         generalizations, or aï¬rmatively contradicted by the record.â Id.         (quotations omitted).                 To show that he is entitled to an evidentiary hearing on his         ineï¬ective-assistance-of-counsel claim, Ivoryâs Â§ 2255 motion must         allege facts that would show (1) âthat counselâs performance was         deï¬cientâ and (2) âthat the deï¬cient performance prejudiced the         defense.â Strickland v. Washington, 466 U.S. 668, 687 (1984); see also         Griï¬th v. United States, 871 F.3d 1321, 1329 (11th Cir. 2017). Ivory         must carry his burden on both prongs, and we âneed not address         both prongs if the defendant has made an insuï¬cient showing on         one.â Osley v. United States, 751 F.3d 1214, 1222 (11th Cir. 2014).                 The âproper measure of attorney performanceâ is âsimply         reasonableness under prevailing professional norms.â Strickland,         466 U.S. at 688. âTo establish deï¬cient performance, a petitioner         must show that counsel made errors so serious that counsel was         not functioning as the âcounselâ guaranteed the defendant by the         Sixth Amendment.â Griï¬th, 871 F.3d at 1329 (quotation omitted).         In other words, the bar for showing deï¬ciency is high.                The same is true for showing prejudice. To do that, Ivory         must demonstrate that âthere is a reasonable probability that, but         for counselâs unprofessional errors, the result of the proceeding         would have been diï¬erent.â Strickland, 466 U.S. at 694. âA         reasonable probability,â in turn, is a probability âsuï¬cient to USCA11 Case: 23-10123     Document: 44-1      Date Filed: 10/03/2025     Page: 13 of 18             23-10123               Opinion of the Court                        13          undermine conï¬dence in the outcome.â Id. Whatâs more, â[t]he         likelihood of a diï¬erent result must be substantial, not just         conceivable.â Harrington v. Richter, 562 U.S. 86, 112 (2011).                 When it comes to challenges involving plea agreements, âa         defendant must show the outcome of the plea process would have         been diï¬erent with competent advice.â Laï¬er v. Cooper, 566 U.S.         156, 163 (2012). And in a situation like the one we have hereâ         where the allegedly ineï¬ective advice âled not to an oï¬erâs         acceptance but to its rejectionââa defendant must show that three         things would have happened âbut for the ineï¬ective advice of         counsel.â Id. at 163â64. First, that there is a reasonable probability         that âthe defendant would have accepted the plea and the         prosecution would not have withdrawn it.â Id. at 164. Second, that         âthe court would have accepted its terms.â Id. And third, that         under the rejected plea oï¬er âthe conviction or sentence, or         both . . . would have been less severeâ than what the defendant         received after trial. Id.                  We do not take the government to dispute that Ivoryâs         counsel was deï¬cient. It would be hard-pressed to do soâthe         Florida Bar explicitly referenced counselâs conduct in this very case         as it began the process of disbarring her. See Formal Complaint for         Reciprocal Discipline at 3, Florida Bar v. Dickerson, No. SC19-616         (Fla. Apr. 16, 2019). So we need not belabor the point: it was not         âreasonableâ for Ivoryâs attorney to tell him that she had secured         two witnesses to testify on his behalf when she had not so much as         contacted either one. Strickland, 466 U.S. at 688. USCA11 Case: 23-10123      Document: 44-1      Date Filed: 10/03/2025      Page: 14 of 18             14                      Opinion of the Court                  23-10123                  Still, that is only the ï¬rst part of the analysis. When it comes         to prejudice, Ivoryâs argument falters. The reason is simple: he         cannot show that he âwould have accepted the pleaâ without his         deï¬cient counsel. Laï¬er, 566 U.S. at 164. In fact, Ivoryâs insistence         that he would have taken the plea is âaï¬rmatively contradicted by         the record.â Winthrop-Redin, 767 F.3d at 1216 (quotation omitted).         Ivory repeatedly maintained that he was innocent of all charges         and insisted that he had nothing to do with the robberies. Whatâs         more, this actual-innocence defense was not a spur-of-the-moment         trial decisionâIvory ï¬led a pretrial motion swearing that he had an         alibi on the night of each robbery.                 Ivory continued to maintain his innocence even after he was         convicted on all counts, pleading with the sentencing judge that he         was ânot a robberâ and that it âwas not [him] in those robberies.â         He explained that he rejected the governmentâs plea oï¬ers because         his âmind wouldnât let [him] admit to something [he] didnât do.â         And he accused Wingster of lying, insisting that a person in jail         âwill say anything to get [himself ] home as soon as possible.â An         interesting assertion under the circumstances.                 In short: Ivory âpersistently refused to accept responsibility         and adamantly professed his innocence during all stages of his         criminal proceedings.â Rosin v. United States, 786 F.3d 873, 878 (11th         Cir. 2015). His choices at trial âreï¬ected an inï¬nite resolve to         proclaim his innocence; they did not manifest any intentionâ to         âaccept responsibility for the conduct alleged.â Id. at 879. And even         during his sentencing hearing, when Ivory was âaï¬orded the USCA11 Case: 23-10123      Document: 44-1      Date Filed: 10/03/2025     Page: 15 of 18             23-10123               Opinion of the Court                         15          opportunity to make a statement to the court and to, perhaps,         accept personal responsibility for the conduct alleged,â he declined         to do so. Id.                  Given all that, we have little diï¬culty concluding that âthe         record evidence patently contradictsâ Ivoryâs assertion that, but for         his trial counselâs error, âhe would have accepted a guilty plea and         not insisted on going to trial.â Id. Without any evidence apart         from his own âconclusory after-the-fact assertionââdiscounted by         the copious ârecord evidence contradictingâ that assertionâthe         district court did not abuse its discretion in declining to hold an         evidentiary hearing. Id.; see also Diaz v. United States, 930 F.2d 832,         835 (11th Cir. 1991) (âafter the fact testimonyâ insuï¬cient to         establish prejudice).                                            B.                Ivory also argues that his attorneyâs failure to call McCant as         a witness rendered his defense constitutionally defective. But this         argument fails in the same way as the last: Ivory cannot show         prejudice. Thatâs true for two reasons: it is highly unlikely that         McCant would have testiï¬ed, and even if he had, the end result         would have been the same.                 When a defendant raises an ineffective assistance claim         based on counselâs failure to call a witness, the defendant carries a         âheavyâ burden to show prejudice. Sullivan v. DeLoach, 459 F.3d         1097, 1109 (11th Cir. 2006). Thatâs because âoften allegations of USCA11 Case: 23-10123      Document: 44-1       Date Filed: 10/03/2025       Page: 16 of 18             16                      Opinion of the Court                    23-10123          what a witness would have testified to are largely speculative.â Id.         (quotation omitted). And here the risk of pure speculation is even         greater because it was âhighly unlikelyâ that McCant would have         testified in the first place. Boyd v. Estelle, 661 F.2d 388, 390 (5th Cir.         1981). After all, he was âcharged with participating in the same         robber[ies]â as Ivory, and his own appeal was still pending during         Ivoryâs trial. Id. Simply put: there is little in the record showing         that McCant âwas willing to testify and waive his Fifth Amendment         privilege against self-incrimination.â                  Indeed, McCant faced several âsignificant tactical issuesâ         when it came to testifying at Ivoryâs trial. For one, if McCant had         testified on Ivoryâs behalf, that would have jeopardized his own         pending appeal. For another, McCant (who was charged with         crimes related to all but the third robbery) might have unwittingly         âimplicate[d] himself in an as-yet uncharged robberyâ during his         cross-examination. And for another still, McCant would have         exposed himself to a future perjury charge if he had lied on the         stand. Given these risks, we cannot imagine that any competent         attorney would have advised McCant to testify, rather than try to         talk him out of itâas Ivoryâs counsel herself acknowledged at oral         argument.                 But even if McCant had testiï¬ed, we think that testimony         would have done his cousin more harm than good. Recall that         Ivoryâs entire defense was that he was positively innocent of all         charges. McCantâs testimony would not have bolstered that         defenseâit would have taken a sledgehammer to it. McCantâs USCA11 Case: 23-10123     Document: 44-1     Date Filed: 10/03/2025    Page: 17 of 18             23-10123              Opinion of the Court                       17          now-revealed testimony is that Ivory was not involved in the ï¬rst         robbery; he does not deny Ivoryâs participation in the second and         third robberies. His silence on those two is telling. What would a         jury have made of the inconsistency between Ivoryâs protestations         of absolute innocence and his cousinâs testimony tying Ivory to the         second and third robberies? Though it would be âlargely         speculativeâ to guessâthatâs one problem with Ivoryâs argumentâ         we donât see how it would have helped him. Sullivan, 459 F.3d at         1109 (quotation omitted).                 And even putting those concerns aside, the âabsence of         exculpatory witness testimonyâ is more likely to prejudice a         defendant when there is âlittle record evidence of guilt.â         Fortenberry v. Haley, 297 F.3d 1213, 1228 (11th Cir. 2002). But here         we have the oppositeâsubstantial record evidence of Ivoryâs guilt.                 First, recall that Wingster testiï¬ed point-blank that Ivory         participated in the ï¬rst and second robberies, and even identiï¬ed         Ivory as he walked the jury through the Walmart surveillance         footage. Cell-site data corroborated this testimony for the second         robbery, and it put Ivory near the third robbery as well. Second was         the ï¬urry of unusual phone calls between Wingster, McCant, and         Ivory leading up to the ï¬rst robberyâcalls that seemed especially         suspicious because Wingster tried to hide his number when he         placed them. Third, McCantâs ï¬rst call when he got to jail was to         Ivoryâs mother, who he told to make sure that Ivory would âstay         where the fuck he at.â Ivoryâs mother dutifully relayed the         message. USCA11 Case: 23-10123        Document: 44-1        Date Filed: 10/03/2025        Page: 18 of 18             18                        Opinion of the Court                     23-10123                  Given all that, the chance that McCantâs testimony would         have led to a diï¬erent result at Ivoryâs trial was a far cry from         âsubstantial.â Harrington, 562 U.S. at 112. The district court thus         did not abuse its discretion in declining to conduct an evidentiary         hearing for his Â§ 2255 claim. In the end, the âï¬les and records of         the case conclusively show that the prisoner is entitled to no         relief.â2 28 U.S.C. Â§ 2255(b).
summary: Over the summer of 2017, the suspect and two accomplices robbed two Walmart stores at gunpoint and attempted a third, wearing masks, forcing store managers or customers to the ground, taking about $100,000 total, and fleeing in stolen cars. The suspect personally held a gun to a manager's head during one robbery and controlled hostages at gunpoint during another. Investigators identified the suspect through an accomplice's cooperation, cell-phone location data placing him near two targeted stores, and suspicious phone call patterns before the first robbery.

caseName: State v. Fletes
plain_text: No. 11                     February 5, 2026                            861                 IN THE SUPREME COURT OF THE                      STATE OF OREGON                    STATE OF OREGON,                      Plaintiff-Relator,                              v.            DOMINIC AGAPITO EARL FLETES,       aka Dominic Fletes, aka Dominic Agapito Fletes,              aka Dominic Agapito E. Fletes,                 Defendant-Adverse Party.         (CC 22CR09099, 22CR09574) (SC S072586)     En Banc    On petition for writ of mandamus filed January 16, 2026; considered and under advisement on February 3, 2026.*     Jennifer S. Lloyd, Assistant Attorney General, Salem, filed the petition for writ of mandamus for plaintiff-relator. Also on the petition were Dan Rayfield, Attorney General, and Paul L. Smith, Solicitor General.    Thaddeus Betz, Oregon Justice Resource Center, Youth Justice Project, Portland, filed the response to the petition for defendant-adverse party.    PER CURIAM    The petition for writ of mandamus is denied.    Bushong, J., dissented and filed an opinion.     ____________    * On petition from an order of the Jackson County Circuit Court, Laura A. Cromwell, Judge. 862   State v. Fletes Cite as 374 Or 861 (2026)                                                     863             PER CURIAM.            The petition for writ of mandamus is denied.            BUSHONG, J., dissenting.          I would have issued the alternative writ of manda- mus and, if the trial court adhered to its decision, I would set this case for briefing and argument on the merits.1 Relator sought relief in the trial court under ORS 137.172 to âcorrectâ or âmodifyâ what relator contended were âerro- neousâ terms in the judgments that had been entered in defendantâs criminal cases.2 Those judgments imposed two consecutive 13-month prison sentences in one case, and a consecutive 30-month prison sentence in another case, for a total prison sentence of 56 months. In relatorâs view, those judgments were âerroneousâ because they did not clearly indicate whether the court was ordering presentence incarceration credit to be applied once towards defendantâs 56-month prison sentence or multiple times to each of the separate consecutive prison sentences. As I will explain, that is a plausible argument under ORS 137.071, a statute that relator did not cite in its petition.          After defendant was sentenced, the Department of Corrections (DOC) applied defendantâs presentence incar- ceration credits once toward defendantâs 56-month prison sentence. Then, after this courtâs decision in State ex rel Torres-Lopez v. Fahrion, 373 Or 816, 572 P3d 1045, adhâd to as modified on recons, 374 Or 423, 579 P3d 1056 (2025), DOC recalculated defendantâs sentences to apply those cred- its multiple times to each of the consecutive sentences that had been imposed by the sentencing court. That recalcula- tion led DOC to release defendant from prison. DOC then changed its interpretation of the sentencing documents, concluding that its original interpretation had been correct      1        Issuing an alternative writ does not mean that we have decided the merits of the petition. See HotChalk, Inc. v. Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod, 372 Or 249, 256, 548 P3d 812 (2024) (noting that the fact that this court âissued an alter- native writ at the outset of a mandamus proceedingâ does not resolve the merits of whether the trial court had a legal duty to act or whether the party seeking relief has another means of recourse that is plain, speedy, and adequate).      2        The adverse party in this mandamus case was the criminal defendant in the underlying criminal cases. For ease of reference, I refer to the adverse party here as âdefendant.â 864                                            State v. Fletes  after all. Based on that subsequent recalculation, DOC ordered defendantâs arrest pursuant to ORS 144.350 so that he could finish serving the remainder of his 56-month prison sentence.          In response to habeas petitions filed by defendant and others who were similarly situated, this court deter- mined that ORS 144.350 did not authorize DOC to sum- marily arrest and imprison those defendants and, therefore, we ordered DOC to release them from custody. See Fletes v. Thrasher, 374 Or 735, __ P3d __ (2026); McEwen v. Thrasher, 374 Or 744, __ P3d __ (2026); Hatton v. Sundquist, 374 Or 739, __ P3d __ (2026); Arellano-Sanchez v. Thrasher, 374 Or 623, ___ P3d ___ (2025); Allen v. Thrasher, 374 Or 618, ___ P3d ___ (2025); Hernandez v. Thrasher, 374 Or 643, ___ P3d ___ (2025). Relator then filed its motion to correct or modify the judgments in defendantâs criminal cases. The trial court denied relatorâs motion, concluding that the original judg- ments may have been ambiguous, but they were not âerro- neous,â and, thus, the court did not believe that ORS 137.172 gave it any authority to correct or modify those judgments.          Determining whether ORS 137.172 gave the trial court that authority would require us to interpret the stat- ute, applying our familiar methodology based on the stat- utory text, context, and any relevant legislative history. State v. Gaines, 346 Or 160, 206 P3d 1042 (2009). The most relevant context, in my view, is ORS 137.071(2)(g), which requires a judgment document in a criminal case to â[s]pec- ify clearly the courtâs disposition, including all legal conse- quences the court establishes or imposes.â DOCâs apparent confusion over whether the original judgment documents required it to apply presentence incarceration credit once or multiple times to the consecutive sentences imposed by the court suggests that those judgment documents did not âspecify clearlyâ all the legal consequences of the prison sen- tences that the court had imposed. In that sense, at least, the judgment documents may have been âerroneous.â It would seem to follow, in my view, that the trial court would have authority under ORS 137.172 to consider correcting or modifying the erroneous terms in those judgment doc- uments and make the legal consequences of the sentences Cite as 374 Or 861 (2026)                                 865  clear. I would issue an alternative writ of mandamus, and if the trial court adhered to its decision, I would set the matter for briefing and argument so that we could resolve the issue on its merits.          Unfortunately, relator did not address ORS 137.071(2)(g) in its petition, and none of the cases cited by the parties have considered how ORS 137.071(2)(g) in con- junction with ORS 137.172 might affect the analysis. That should not, in my view, preclude us from requesting briefing on the issue so that we can resolve it in this mandamus case. Nor should the courtâs decision declining to issue an alterna- tive writ in this case preclude consideration of the issue in a future case.         Accordingly, I respectfully dissent from this courtâs decision to deny the petition for a writ of mandamus.
